name: Delian League
info: A confederacy of between 150 and 330 Greek city-states under Athenian hegemony, founded in 478 BC to continue the war against Persia, which became the naval empire known as the Athenian Empire.

facts.capital: Delos (congresses and treasury), then Athens (treasury from 454 BC)
facts.founder: Athens, at a congress on Delos; Aristides set the members' tax
facts.predecessor: The Hellenic alliance that fought Xerxes I's invasion
facts.successor: Spartan hegemony; later the Second Athenian League (377 BC)

t: The Delian League was founded in 478 BC on the island of Delos to continue the fight against the Persian Empire after the Battle of Plataea.
Most members chose to pay a tax to the joint treasury rather than supply ships, and Athens used the funds to build up its own navy.
In 454 BC Pericles moved the treasury from Delos to Athens, and tribute paid to the league funded building on the Acropolis, including the Parthenon.
dyk: League members swore to have the same friends and enemies and dropped ingots of iron into the sea to symbolize the permanence of their alliance.
ev: After Sparta withdraws from the war, a congress on Delos founds a new alliance under Athens
Naxos becomes the first member to attempt to secede and is defeated
Thasos defects to Persia and is forced back into the league after more than two years of siege
Athens sends 250 ships to aid the Egyptian revolt of Inaros and Amyrtaeus, an expedition that ends in heavy losses
Pericles moves the league's treasury from Delos to Athens
A peace with Persia, known as the Peace of Callias, is reported, though some writers believe the treaty a later myth
The Peloponnesian War breaks out between the Delian and Peloponnesian Leagues
The league is dissolved at the end of the Peloponnesian War, under the direction of Lysander

sections.foundation:
The Greco-Persian Wars began with the conquest of the Greek cities of Ionia by the Achaemenid Persian Empire of Cyrus the Great shortly after 550 BC. After the Ionian Revolt and two Persian invasions of Greece, the Allies defeated the forces of Xerxes I at the Battle of Plataea and the Battle of Mycale in 479 BC, then took Sestos and, in 478 BC, Byzantion. The behaviour of the Spartan general Pausanias alienated many of the Allies and led to his recall.

Sparta was eager to end its involvement in the war. Its king Leotychidas had proposed moving the Greeks of Asia Minor to Europe, which the Athenian commander Xanthippus rejected: the Ionian cities had been Athenian colonies, and the Athenians would protect them. With the Spartan withdrawal, a congress was called on the holy island of Delos to found a new alliance to continue the fight, which gives the league its modern name. Contemporaries called it simply "the Athenians and their Allies". According to Thucydides, its official aim was to "avenge the wrongs they suffered by ravaging the territory of the king." Members swore an oath of loyalty, and the Athenian politician Aristides spent the rest of his life on the affairs of the alliance.
sections.socioeconomy:
The league numbered between 150 and 330 city-states, largely around the Aegean Sea and the coast of Anatolia. Members could either supply armed forces or pay a tax to the joint treasury, and most chose the tax. Thucydides writes that this was their own doing: wishing to avoid service, they paid money, and Athens increased its navy with the funds while any revolt found itself without enough resources or experienced leaders.

The treasury stood first at Delos, where congresses were held within the sanctuary of the Temple of Apollo. In 454 BC Pericles moved it to Athens, allegedly to keep it safe from Persia, and Athens switched from accepting ships, men and weapons as dues to accepting only money. Plutarch indicates that many of Pericles's rivals saw the transfer as usurping the funds for building projects. Tribute paid to the league financed the Parthenon on the Acropolis, replacing an older temple, and many other expenditures unrelated to defence. Defeated rebels paid in land and resources: Thasos lost its land, ships and the mines of Thasos to Athens, and after the revolt of Mytilene the land of Lesbos was redistributed to Athenian shareholders sent to live there.
sections.military:
Athens was the league's biggest source of military power and the dominant naval power of the Greek world. Under Cimon the league expelled the remaining Persian forces from the Aegean, and in its first ten years Cimon forced Karystos in Euboea to join, conquered the island of Skyros and settled Athenian colonists there. In 460 BC Pericles led 250 ships to aid the Egyptian revolt of Inaros and Amyrtaeus; after four years the Achaemenid general Megabyzus defeated the rebellion and captured most of the Athenian force. Isocrates put the losses at some 20,000 men; modern estimates place them at 50,000 men and 250 ships. In 451 BC Cimon led 200 ships to Cyprus and died during the blockade of Citium, though the fleet won a double victory off Salamis, Cyprus, the last major battle against the Persians.

In Greece, the Athenians lost the Battle of Tanagra but won the Battle of Oenophyta and controlled Boeotia except Thebes, until the Battle of Coronea in 447 BC led to its abandonment. The Long Walls joined Athens to the Piraeus. In the Peloponnesian War from 431 BC, Athens suppressed revolts and conquered neutral Melos, putting its men to death and selling its women into slavery.
sections.governance:
The league began as a dual offensive and defensive alliance, or symmachia, of autonomous states, with an assembly of representatives to shape its policy. Many democratic members owed their freedom from oligarchic or tyrannical rule to Athens, which gave Athens an overwhelming advantage in the voting. Over time Athens established complete dominion, and it came to call the members "all the cities Athens rules." It also ruled through the courts: matters within and between states were resolved in Athens by courts of Athenian citizens and enforced by the Athenian military.

Pericles, from 450 BC, set up kleruchiai, quasi-colonies tied to Athens that served as garrisons across the league's territory. A number of offices held the empire together: proxenoi fostered good relations between Athens and the members, episkopoi and archontes oversaw the collection of tribute, and hellenotamiai received the tribute on Athens's behalf. Athenian politics shaped the league's course. In 461 BC Cimon was ostracized and succeeded in influence by democrats such as Ephialtes and Pericles, and Athens turned from alliance with Sparta to alliance with Sparta's enemies, Argos and Thessaly.
sections.impact:
The league achieved its principal strategic goal by expelling the remaining Persian forces from the Aegean, and Persia ceased to pose a major threat to Greece for the following fifty years. After the battle off Salamis, Cyprus, an understanding with Persia was reached, whether or not a formal Peace of Callias was ever made, and Athens turned its attention to Greece.

Within the league, the members lost their autonomy. The siege of Thasos marked the change of the league from an alliance into, in Thucydides's words, a hegemony, and by the mid-fifth century BC it is conventionally called the Athenian Empire. Historians see the moving of the treasury in 454 BC as a key marker of that change, while warning against treating any single event as its main cause. The tribute enriched Athens itself: it reinforced the city's naval supremacy and embellished it with art and architecture, among them the Parthenon. Beyond the Aegean, Megara left the Peloponnesian League to ally with Athens, and a double line of walls was built across the Isthmus of Corinth. The threat the league posed to Spartan hegemony, with Athens's heavy-handed administration, prompted the Peloponnesian War, which drew in much of the Greek world.
sections.decline:
Rebellion ran through the league's history. Naxos tried to secede in c. 471 BC and is believed to have lost its walls, fleet and vote. Thasos defected in 465 BC, after Athens founded the colony of Amphipolis on the Strymon river near its mines of Mt. Pangaion; Sparta, facing the largest helot revolt in its history, refused it aid. Euboea and Megara revolted after 447 BC: Euboea was restored as a tributary ally, Megara permanently lost. A thirty-year peace between the Delian and Peloponnesian Leagues lasted only until 431 BC.

By the start of the Peloponnesian War only Chios and Lesbos still contributed ships. Lesbos revolted and failed; the Athenians ordered the death of the whole male population of Mytilene, then rescinded the order and executed the leading 1000 ringleaders. Chios revolted last, after the Syracusan Expedition, inspiring all of Ionia to revolt, though Athens suppressed these revolts. After 27 years of war the Spartans, aided by the Persians and by strife within Athens, defeated the Athenian empire, and the league was dissolved in 404 BC under the direction of Lysander. Athens revived it in part as the Second Athenian League, founded in 377 BC against Spartan and then Theban hegemony, but never recovered the full extent of its power.

summary: The Delian League was the alliance of Aegean Greek city-states that Athens led against Persia from 478 BC. It drove the Persians from the Aegean, but Athens turned the members' tribute and its fleet into an empire, moved the treasury to Athens in 454 BC and crushed revolts, until defeat in the Peloponnesian War dissolved the league in 404 BC.
references: Russell Meiggs, The Athenian Empire (Clarendon Press, 1972)
Peter John Rhodes, A History of the Classical Greek World: 478–323 BC (Blackwell Publishing, 2006)
Wolfgang Schuller, Die Herrschaft der Athener im Ersten Attischen Seebund (De Gruyter, 1974)
Thomas R. Martin, Ancient Greece: From Prehistoric to Hellenistic Times (Yale University Press, 2000)

pointDescs.-478: After the capture of Byzantion and the Spartan withdrawal, a congress on Delos founds the league under Athens.
pointDescs.-471: Naxos attempts to secede and is defeated, the first member to try.
pointDescs.-465: Thasos defects to Persia and is forced back into the league after more than two years of siege; the league becomes, in Thucydides's words, a hegemony.
pointDescs.-461: Cimon is ostracized; Ephialtes and Pericles lead Athens into alliance with Argos and Thessaly, and Megara joins Athens.
pointDescs.-454: Pericles moves the treasury from Delos to Athens, after the failed expedition to Egypt.
pointDescs.-450: After the double victory off Salamis, Cyprus, an understanding with Persia is reached, and Pericles begins founding kleruchiai.
pointDescs.-447: Defeat at the Battle of Coronea leads to the abandonment of Boeotia; Euboea and Megara revolt.
pointDescs.-431: The Peloponnesian War breaks out with Sparta and its allies.
pointDescs.-413: After the Syracusan Expedition, Chios revolts and inspires all of Ionia to revolt.
pointDescs.-404: Sparta, aided by Persia, defeats Athens and the league is dissolved under the direction of Lysander.

notes: The article gives no references list (its References and Sources sections are empty), so references are [].
The article dates the moving of the treasury both 'by 454' and '454 BC'; I used 454 BC.

413 BC for Chios's revolt is my placing of 'in the aftermath of the Syracusan Expedition'; the article gives no year. The article also says Aristides received Thasos's surrender, which is doubtful (it says he died a few years after 478) but kept out of the text.
The Peace of Callias is hedged as the article hedges it.
